title: The One With The Girl Who Hits Joey

jokes.text: Listen, we had a good run. What was it? Four, five months? That's more than most people have in a lifetime. Goodbye.
jokes.setup: Ross is screaming outside the window having caught Chandler with Monica. Chandler is terrified.
jokes.punchline: Instead of facing Ross, Chandler tries to end the relationship on the spot and flee, framing four months as a full life's worth of love.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Chandler: his cowardice in relationships is a core character trait, and the idea of dumping Monica to escape Ross is both logical within his character and absurd. The deadpan 'That's more than most people have in a lifetime' is a sharp, well-structured line.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You were with Monica?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, I can explain—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No! You said we were friends!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We are friends! This doesn't mean anything!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Doesn't mean anything? Chandler, you're treating our friendship like some casual thing!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not fair—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We're done. I'm out.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: *storms out*

jokes.text: I am going on the lam.
jokes.setup: Monica asks what he's doing as he prepares to flee.
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses a fugitive metaphor ('going on the lam') for hiding from his girlfriend's brother.
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and character-specific. Chandler's overdramatic self-pity expressed through crime-drama vocabulary is very on-brand. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm fleeing the scene. I'm an accessory after the fact. I'm harboring a fugitive... myself.

jokes.text: Dude, he's right there. [said to Ross about Ross]
jokes.setup: Chandler has been caught by Monica whispering 'I think Ross knows about me and Monica' — to Monica — while Ross is standing right there.
jokes.punchline: Joey points out the obvious: 'Dude, he's right there.' The joke is Chandler's oblivious panic causing him to narrate the situation to the wrong person.
jokes.explanation: A quick situational laugh — Chandler's panic has caused him to forget Ross is literally present. Joey's deadpan correction is the right payoff. Functional but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So... how about those Knicks?

jokes.text: Joey, to Ross after the emotional declarations: 'You guys want to probably get some hugs in too. Big news!'
jokes.setup: Ross has just had a huge emotional revelation about his best friend and sister. It's a charged, serious moment.
jokes.punchline: Joey cheerfully suggests group hugs and declares 'Big news!' — treating a loaded emotional moment with the enthusiastic shallowness of a game show host.
jokes.explanation: Very strong Joey moment. His inability to read the room, combined with his genuine warmth, makes 'Big news!' land perfectly. It's character-specific in the best way — only Joey would try to lighten a tense confrontation this way. The exclamatory 'Big news!' is quotable and punchy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So... you're mad?

jokes.text: Okay. All right. Let's clear out of here and let these lovebirds get back to business.
jokes.setup: Ross is having an emotional breakdown upon learning about Chandler and Monica. The moment is tense and dramatic.
jokes.punchline: Joey cheerfully suggests everyone leave so Chandler and Monica can resume what Ross caught them doing — completely missing the room.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey obliviousness — undercutting genuine emotional tension with cheerful cluelessness. Character-integrated and structurally sound.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why would you tell him? Now the whole building's gonna know!

jokes.text: I'm just talking here. He's the one doing your sister.
jokes.setup: Ross is upset at everyone, including Joey, for knowing about Chandler and Monica.
jokes.punchline: Joey deflects by pointing out he's innocent — he wasn't the one sleeping with Ross's sister, implying Chandler is the real target.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The bluntness of 'doing your sister' is a deliberately crude contrast to the emotional moment, landing with the audience because it's so specifically Joey — self-preserving, blunt, and accidental. High quotability, excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, I love you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I love you too.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wow, this is... this is huge.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This calls for a celebration! Who wants to go to Hooters?

jokes.text: Shouldn't her brother be godfather? Sure. If you cared enough to call it first.
jokes.setup: Ross objects that as Monica's brother, he should be godfather to any future children.
jokes.punchline: Joey responds that the godfather position is first-come-first-served, and Ross lost by not calling it.
jokes.explanation: Joey treating godfather like a playground 'dibs' situation is funny and character-specific. The logic is absurd but delivered with total sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm just saying, let the lovebirds get back to business.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, so now it's my fault?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, I'm not the one who broke up with her.

jokes.text: You're a few steps ahead of us. Big zero gravity moon steps.
jokes.setup: Joey and others are already planning weddings and godchildren for Chandler and Monica, who just came out as a couple.
jokes.punchline: Chandler characterizes their friends' leap as 'big zero gravity moon steps' — an oddly specific and evocative image for how far ahead everyone is running.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'zero gravity moon steps' elevates this above a standard deflection. It's a surprising image — not a cliché — and shows the writers reaching for something more distinctive. Good originality score for a sitcom one-liner.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait a minute. You and Chandler... you're gonna have kids, right?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What?! I don't know! Maybe! Why would you—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because I'm gonna be the godfather!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, we haven't even—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I already picked out my godfather outfit. Black suit, white shirt, very intimidating.

jokes.text: I just thought of the greatest wedding gift. — I'll go in on that with you. I couldn't decide.
jokes.setup: Phoebe announces a great wedding gift idea for Chandler and Monica, who have just started dating.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately volunteers to split the gift cost — she also had no idea what to get. Neither of them acknowledges there's no wedding.
jokes.explanation: A quick background joke that lands on the absurdity of everyone getting ahead of themselves. Functional but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Shotgun! I'm the godfather!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You can't call shotgun on being a godfather.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not? I called it first!

jokes.text: She is so cute. You could fit her in your pocket. — She could fit in that little pocket inside the pocket.
jokes.setup: Joey introduces his new girlfriend Katie, who is very small.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe escalates Rachel's pocket comment by specifying the small interior pocket inside jeans — the famously useless tiny pocket.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's escalation of the pocket observation to the tiny inside pocket is a nice specific comedic detail. The 'little pocket inside the pocket' is universally relatable and timed well as a topper.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, you're getting way ahead of yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's not just ahead of himself, he's like... he's on Mars. And himself is still here on Earth. He's so far ahead of himself, NASA is tracking him.

jokes.text: But what? — She keeps punching me.
jokes.setup: Joey says he likes Katie a lot and she's really nice, 'but...' leading the audience to expect a relationship complaint.
jokes.punchline: The complaint is that she physically punches him — a totally unexpected, literal answer.
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection setup. The pause and delivery work well. The premise itself — a tiny woman beating up Joey — is a solid physical comedy engine for the episode's B-plot.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She's so cute!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She's so tiny!

jokes.text: In the cute, little sweet way she just did? — It's a lot harder than it looks.
jokes.setup: Katie has just punched Joey in what looked like a playful tap.
jokes.punchline: Joey winces and insists it's much harder than it appears, implying he's genuinely suffering while everyone assumes it's adorable.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy engine is established here. The gap between how it looks (cute) and how it feels (painful) is the core joke of the subplot, and this line crystallizes it efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, she could fit in my coin purse!

jokes.text: I know what you need. You need a bodyguard. What is Ben doing after preschool?
jokes.setup: Joey is being hurt by his tiny girlfriend. Rachel suggests he needs a bodyguard.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately follows up by suggesting Ross's toddler son Ben as the bodyguard candidate.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's non sequitur logic — responding seriously to a joke with an even more absurd solution — is perfect Phoebe. The specificity of 'What is Ben doing after preschool?' lands the joke hard. Excellent economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She's adorable, but... I don't know, man. Something about her just bothers me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? She's tiny! What could possibly be wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's the thing — she keeps punching me. Like, full force. In the arm.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She's five feet tall, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know! That's what makes it so humiliating!

jokes.text: Joey is having a problem. A little girl is beating him up.
jokes.setup: Phoebe relays Joey's situation to someone off-screen, apparently Ross.
jokes.punchline: The blunt, matter-of-fact delivery of 'a little girl is beating him up' as a serious problem report is inherently comic.
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the deadpan delivery of an absurd summary. Functional joke that keeps the physical comedy subplot alive.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't believe Katie hurt me! She's like three feet tall!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, why don't you hire Ross's son Ben as your bodyguard? He's in preschool.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ben? He's like five years old!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Exactly. Katie wouldn't stand a chance.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, am I hurting you? [Monica punches Joey while expressing sympathy]
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to empathize with Joey about being hit by his girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: While delivering sympathy, Monica herself hits Joey — the visual irony of being hurt by the person comforting you about being hurt.
jokes.explanation: The structural irony here is well-executed — the person meant to give comfort inflicts the same pain being complained about. It's a visual gag that works perfectly in the multi-camera format where the audience sees both the punch and Joey's reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So Joey's been living in Monica's apartment this whole time, and he doesn't even pay rent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? He's been here for months!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's so Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, and get this - he told me he thought the rent was optional.

jokes.text: Salt, so your life always has flavor. Bread, so you never go hungry. And a scented candle for the bathroom. Because, well, you know.
jokes.setup: Phoebe presents Ross with traditional housewarming gifts with increasingly elaborate poetic justifications.
jokes.punchline: The third gift — a scented candle 'for the bathroom, because, well, you know' — deflates the ceremony of the first two with a crude, unspoken implication.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured rule of three. The first two gifts are presented with earnest spiritual gravitas, making the pivot to 'scented candle for the bathroom, because, well, you know' land perfectly. The understated 'you know' does the heavy lifting — Phoebe is implying Ross's bathroom smells. Excellent structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know how hard this must be for you, Joey. People can be so cruel—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ow!

jokes.text: Mr. President.
jokes.setup: Steve introduces himself as president of the tenants' committee.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe greets him with the formal address 'Mr. President,' playing along with his self-importance with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Two words that do maximum work. Phoebe's total sincerity here is the joke — she's not being sarcastic, she's genuinely respecting the title. Economy score is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I brought you some housewarming gifts with traditional meanings. This bread is for prosperity, this salt is for flavor, and this plunger is for when you realize you have a weird pipe situation.

jokes.text: Well, the guy's worked here for 25 years. — Yes, but I've lived here for 25 minutes.
jokes.setup: The building committee president guilts Ross into contributing to the handyman's retirement fund.
jokes.punchline: Ross's parallel construction — matching '25 years' with '25 minutes' — is a sharp, economical rebuttal.
jokes.explanation: One of the cleaner jokes of the episode. The parallel structure ('25 years' / '25 minutes') is elegant and the logic, while flawed, is delivered with such conviction it works. Classic comedy economy — maximum impact, minimum words.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're the president? Of the building?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's like... that's like being the president of the country, but for a building.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You must have so much power. And responsibility.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Do you have a limo? Does the building give you a limo?

jokes.text: Howard's the handyman. — Yes, but to me, he's just 'man.'
jokes.setup: Ross protests he doesn't know Howard. Steve clarifies that Howard is the handyman.
jokes.punchline: Ross's rebuttal — that Howard is just 'man' to him, since he can't specify his trade — is a pedantic, wordplay-based deflection that shows his stubborn intellectual vanity.
jokes.explanation: Very Ross — using intellectual wordplay to win a petty argument. The 'handyman' / 'man' distinction is precisely the kind of pedantic logic Ross would deploy, and the economy of delivery makes it land clean.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Howard's been here for 20 years, so he should contribute more.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I've been here for 20 minutes, so I should contribute less.

jokes.text: Can you believe that guy? — I really like his glasses.
jokes.setup: Ross is outraged after the confrontation with Steve. He turns to Phoebe for validation.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe, instead of validating, shares that she likes Steve's glasses — a complete non-sequitur that reveals she was barely listening.
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe response — she's in her own world. The specificity of the glasses (not 'I like him' but the precise detail of his glasses) makes this feel fresh rather than a generic non-sequitur. Great character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't know who Howard is.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: Howard's the guy who works in the building.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, to me he's just some guy.

jokes.text: And told me to wipe it off with my $100 bill. — You really should wipe it off with something.
jokes.setup: Ross explains that a kid spit on his knee and sarcastically told him to wipe it with his money.
jokes.punchline: Joey ignores the sarcasm entirely and responds practically — yes, Ross should wipe it off — missing the point completely.
jokes.explanation: Joey's oblivious literalism is a reliable comic engine. Not the sharpest version of the joke but it works in the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean, can you believe how unreasonable Steve is being?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, but those pants are really working for him.

jokes.text: I am not a cheap guy. I'm just a guy who stands up for what he believes in. A man with principles. — Sounds like a fun party.
jokes.setup: Ross delivers an increasingly grandiose self-justification for not giving $100.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's dry 'Sounds like a fun party' punctures the whole speech — implying a party built around defending Ross's principles will be terrible.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's four-word deflation of Ross's self-righteous monologue is well-timed and perfectly dry. The understatement works because the audience already knows this party is a terrible idea.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Even the children in the building hate me. Yesterday, a kid looked at me and said, 'There goes Ross, he's so cheap he won't even buy himself a new sweater.'

jokes.text: If you want them to like you, why don't you just pay the $100? The party will cost you more. — That doesn't matter! It's my principles! We're talking about my principles!
jokes.setup: Phoebe offers the logical solution — just pay the $100.
jokes.punchline: Ross's escalating outrage about 'principles' while explicitly rejecting fiscal logic reveals he's being completely irrational. The repetition of 'my principles' is the gag.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ross stubbornness joke. The gap between his stated values (principles) and his actual behavior (obsessing about $100) is well-worn Ross territory. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, at least he didn't spit in your mouth. That's how you get mono.

jokes.text: I thought it was about your neighbors liking you. — They'll like me once they come to my awesome party.
jokes.setup: Ross contradicts himself — he said it was about principles, but earlier framed it as wanting neighbors to like him.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately pivots back to wanting to be liked, undermining his entire 'principles' speech.
jokes.explanation: The contradiction exposes Ross's self-delusion neatly, but it's a relatively predictable beat following the 'principles' joke. Diminishing returns on the same joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why don't you just buy new furniture?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's way cheaper than paying someone to fix it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, it's not about the money, Phoebe. It's about being right.

jokes.text: And that crazy party animal will be your brother-in-law.
jokes.setup: Ross has just dramatically declared he's throwing a party and gone off for nametags.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, to Monica, deadpans that this is the man who will be her brother-in-law — using Ross's absurdity to both mock Ross and deflect from the marriage implication.
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: mocking Ross and inadvertently acknowledging the marriage subtext. Chandler's self-aware delivery would sell this.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, so you want to throw a party but you don't want anyone to have fun?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, that's not what I said. I'm an excellent party host. I throw great parties.

jokes.text: Very funny. But don't say that to Monica. Don't put any ideas in her head.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just made the brother-in-law joke and is now worried about Monica overhearing.
jokes.punchline: His terror that Monica might start thinking about marriage reveals his commitment phobia even as he's supposedly in a healthy relationship.
jokes.explanation: Sets up the Chandler commitment-phobia subplot but isn't particularly funny on its own. Character-integrated but structurally weak.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, a crazy party animal.

jokes.text: I'm completely different from Richard. He's an eye doctor, and I don't wear glasses.
jokes.setup: Joey has just pointed out that Monica left Richard because he didn't want babies, and Monica wants babies. Chandler insists he's different from Richard.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's only evidence that he's different from Richard is that one is an eye doctor and Chandler doesn't wear glasses — a gloriously non-sequitur, irrelevant distinction.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The logic is perfectly Chandler: panicked, reaching for any distinction to avoid the terrifying parallel between himself and Richard. The fact that his only defense is 'he's an eye doctor and I don't wear glasses' is both deeply character-specific and laugh-out-loud absurd. High quotability, strong rewatch value. Comparable to the calibration anchors for an 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Monica doesn't want to get married. She just... likes to plan things. And babies? She just thinks they're cute. It's not like she's been dropping hints or anything.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler, she literally just said she wants to get married and have babies.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, but she didn't *mean* it like that.

jokes.text: You're right. You're absolutely right. That makes everything different. — It's not different, is it? — Not unless different means 'the same.'
jokes.setup: Joey sarcastically agrees with Chandler's glasses argument to get him to calm down.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately sees through it and asks. Joey's final line — 'Not unless different means the same' — is a perfectly constructed tautological non-answer.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to joke 25. 'Not unless different means the same' is a genuinely clever construction — using tautological logic to confirm the bad news gently. Well-structured exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not like Richard! I'm completely different. I'm younger, I have less money, and I'm way less mature.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Plus, I don't own a boat, I've never performed surgery, and I've certainly never dated Monica before... well, until now.

jokes.text: You were so funny with that waiter. You're such a nut! — You know, bread-stick fangs are always funny. — No, you make them funny. You're the funny one!
jokes.setup: Katie is lavishing Joey with praise in an affectionate moment.
jokes.punchline: The exchange about bread-stick fangs establishes that Joey thinks of himself as inherently funny, while the irony for the audience is that this adorable woman is about to get broken up with.
jokes.explanation: Functional scene-setting but not a strong joke in itself. The bread-stick fangs detail is charming but doesn't punch very hard.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're nothing like Richard.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? How so?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, for starters, Richard is successful.

jokes.text: But sometimes when you playfully punch me like that... it feels like I'm being hit with a very tiny but a very real bat!
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to tell Katie, as gently as possible, that her playful punches hurt.
jokes.punchline: The image of 'a very tiny but a very real bat' is a vivid, specific, and funny metaphor that balances the need to soften the complaint while still making clear it's serious.
jokes.explanation: The 'tiny but real bat' image is specific enough to be memorable. Joey's diplomatic effort to soften the complaint while still being honest is funny in itself, and the metaphor lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, breadsticks are funny.

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: Oh Joey, you're so smart and handsome! Your observations are brilliant!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Like I could hurt you. — Are you making fun of my size? Don't make fun of me because of my size!
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to tell Katie she's hurting him. Katie completely misreads it as mockery of her small stature.
jokes.punchline: The reversal — the person causing pain accusing the victim of mockery — is the comedic engine, and Katie's indignation escalates the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The reversal works well — Joey can't win because his complaint about being hurt is taken as an insult. The trap tightens nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's like being hit by a very tiny but very real bat.

jokes.text: Couldn't you just stay here forever? — Yeah, here, somewhere else. You know, wherever.
jokes.setup: Monica, in an intimate moment, asks if Chandler could stay there forever — a loaded statement.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately deflects the 'forever' implication by making it generic — 'here, somewhere else, wherever' — a classic commitment dodge.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Chandler — the moment calls for romantic reciprocity and he responds with 'somewhere else, wherever.' The character integration is excellent; this joke only works for Chandler.

jokes.text: Just hanging out. Having fun with the girl that I'm seeing casually.
jokes.setup: Monica asks if Chandler is okay after his deflection. He's clearly performing casual indifference.
jokes.punchline: The performed casualness of 'seeing casually' — referring to his serious girlfriend — reveals his panic about commitment.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's overcorrection into 'casual' territory is funny and character-specific but a beat that's predictable for his character.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Could you stay in bed with me forever?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can stay until like, 11.

jokes.text: Man, I knew it! I knew you'd do this. — What? — Get all freaked out because everybody was joking about marriage!
jokes.setup: Monica has seen through Chandler's casualness and calls out his behavior directly.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is that Monica is so right, so quickly, and Chandler has nowhere to hide — the comedy is in his total exposure.
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic beat than a pure joke, but the audience's delight in Monica seeing through Chandler so immediately qualifies as comedy. Mid-range.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Nothing! Just hanging out. You know, casual. Very casual. Just me, being casual. Casually casual.

jokes.text: You know what I want? — Yes! You want babies! You have baby fever!
jokes.setup: Monica is about to explain what she wants from their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Chandler panics and blurts out his fears before she can speak — projecting his commitment terror onto her.
jokes.explanation: 'Baby fever' is a funny specific phrase and Chandler's catastrophizing is on-brand. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you think I want all that stuff?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No! No, of course not. You're gonna be a great mother. You're gonna be nurturing, and caring, and... and all of those things that mothers are.

jokes.text: Why don't we turn the heat down on this pressure cooker!
jokes.setup: Chandler is spiraling in his argument with Monica about commitment.
jokes.punchline: His use of 'pressure cooker' as a metaphor for the conversation is a typical Chandler over-expression — he's both deflecting and describing his internal state.
jokes.explanation: A mild laugh line. The metaphor is a bit clichéd even if the delivery would sell it. Below average for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I think we need to turn down the heat here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Turn down the heat? You're the one who keeps stirring the pot!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, maybe we should let this simmer for a bit instead of letting it boil over.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you want to simmer?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes! Before someone gets burned. And I'm not talking about the casserole.

jokes.text: You don't know everything. — Did you know I'm going out with Rachel tonight instead of you? And that the only baby here is you? Did you know I can't even look at you now?
jokes.setup: Chandler claims Monica doesn't know everything about him.
jokes.punchline: Monica fires back with three devastating rapid-fire 'Did you know' statements, each escalating — capping with 'the only baby here is you' and refusing to look at him.
jokes.explanation: Monica's structured takedown — using the same rhetorical device three times with escalation — is tight writing. 'The only baby here is you' is a sharp insult with good sting. The structure gives it comedic rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The only baby here is you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're done.

jokes.text: I did not know that.
jokes.setup: Monica has told Chandler she can't look at him after their fight.
jokes.punchline: Chandler responds with quiet, defeated understatement — 'I did not know that' — a callback to Monica's rhetorical 'Did you know' structure, using it against himself.
jokes.explanation: Four words doing exceptional work. Chandler picks up Monica's own rhetorical device and turns it on himself with a defeated self-awareness that is both funny and poignant. The economy is near-perfect, and it's deeply character-specific — only Chandler would respond to being shut down by quietly, sincerely noting 'I did not know that.' Strong candidate for the episode's best single line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't look at you.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay.

jokes.text: It'll be okay, right? She won't leave me. This is fixable. — Yeah, sure. — Absolutely. — By me?
jokes.setup: Chandler seeks reassurance from Joey and Ross that his relationship with Monica is fixable.
jokes.punchline: After getting two quick 'sure/absolutely' responses, Chandler asks 'By me?' — realizing the reassurance didn't include him actually being capable of fixing anything.
jokes.explanation: The 'By me?' topper is an excellent Chandler beat — the boys say yes without thinking, and Chandler's self-doubt is so deep he immediately questions whether he personally is the right person to fix it. Tight structure, great economy, very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Who are 'these guys'? Your friends who think a high-five is an acceptable way to end a conversation?

jokes.text: Unless you make some big gesture. / Big, though.
jokes.setup: Joey and Ross advise Chandler that the situation is fixable if he makes a big gesture.
jokes.punchline: Ross's unnecessary addendum 'Big, though' — adding emphasis to a word Joey already used — is funny in its earnestness. They're both terrible advisors.
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh. The redundant 'Big, though' from Ross is a quick hit, suggesting their advice is not exactly sophisticated. Works as a small beat in the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You two are the worst relationship advisors ever.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, you're probably right.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey! Speak for yourself!

jokes.text: I'm really tired of being your relationship tutor. Figure this out for yourself.
jokes.setup: Chandler comes to Monica and asks her to tell him how to fix things — apparently a pattern.
jokes.punchline: Monica calling herself his 'relationship tutor' frames their entire dynamic as educational — she's been coaching him through basic relationship behavior repeatedly.
jokes.explanation: 'Relationship tutor' is a fresh and specific term that captures Monica and Chandler's dynamic with economy. Character-integrated and funny in its accuracy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What would you have done if I said yes?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I would've run out of here so fast, there would've been a Chandler-shaped hole in that door. My feet would still be spinning when I got to the street.

jokes.text: What are you doing here? I thought this was your party, and it's a party for Howard.
jokes.setup: Ross threw a party to win over his neighbors. He arrives to find it's become a Howard the handyman retirement party.
jokes.punchline: Ross's party has been hijacked — his attempt to be liked has been subsumed by the very cause he was refusing to support.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural irony — the party Ross threw to avoid contributing to Howard's retirement has become Howard's retirement party. Classic situational comedy payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I like being the mysterious benefactor. It makes me feel like Batman.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you just gave them fifty dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Fifty dollars worth of hope, Monica. Fifty dollars worth of hope.

jokes.text: I thought you agreed it was unreasonable that they asked me for that money. — But they didn't ask me. I'm just the exotic, generous stranger. That's always fun to be.
jokes.setup: Ross is upset that Phoebe gave $100 when she seemed to agree with his position.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe explains she's playing the role of 'exotic, generous stranger' — a character she enjoys inhabiting — revealing she has no ideological stake, just aesthetic preference.
jokes.explanation: 'The exotic, generous stranger. That's always fun to be' is excellent Phoebe — she's not making a principled choice, she's playing a character she enjoys. The phrase 'exotic, generous stranger' is specific, surprising, and very Phoebe. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Well, I didn't do it on purpose.

jokes.text: I'm not making you look bad! If anything, I'm making you look better. They'll see you talking to me. I'm a hit.
jokes.setup: Ross complains that Phoebe giving money makes him look worse by comparison.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's logic — that people seeing Ross talk to her (a popular person) will improve his standing by association — is both self-aggrandizing and completely missing the point.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's oblivious self-confidence is played well. 'I'm a hit' as a declaration is funny. Solid mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Is my padding obvious?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, it's not obvious. But it is mysterious.

jokes.text: Hey, Phoebe! — Hey, Ross. — Maybe you two could switch apartments. Because Phoebe is more our kind of people. Think about it.
jokes.setup: A neighbor enthusiastically greets Phoebe at Ross's own party.
jokes.punchline: The neighbor suggests Phoebe move in instead of Ross — confirming that Ross's attempt to be liked has resulted in Phoebe being liked in his place.
jokes.explanation: A good situational payoff — Ross's plan has backfired so spectacularly that someone is literally suggesting Phoebe take his apartment. The escalation lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, this girl is crazy. When I break up with her, she's gonna hit me so hard.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what's the problem?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The problem is I really like her! I got feelings for her!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You? Feelings?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! I'm in love with her, okay? I'm in love with Katie!

jokes.text: Hey, Phoebe! / Hey, Ross. / Maybe you two could switch apartments. Because Phoebe is more our kind of people.
jokes.setup: The building neighbors love Phoebe (who gave $100) and hate Ross (who didn't).
jokes.punchline: A neighbor suggests Phoebe move in instead — openly telling Ross, to his face, that his friend is more welcome than he is.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the humiliation. The neighbors' preference for Phoebe over Ross, expressed directly to Ross, is a strong situational beat. 'Our kind of people' is good — implies Ross is an outsider in his own home.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Joey love.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more in love with yourself?

jokes.text: You look big. — Thanks, I've been working out. — Listen, is it obvious I'm wearing six sweaters?
jokes.setup: Rachel notices Joey looks unusually large.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he's wearing six sweaters as padding before breaking up with Katie — the visual of a visibly padded Joey is the gag.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Joey wearing six sweaters as breakup protection is an inspired physical comedy bit. His deadpan 'Thanks, I've been working out' before the reveal is a perfect misdirection. Very Joey, very physical, and the image is memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, we're not for everyone. But Joey loves us, and that's what matters.

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: I just think you're all so... intense.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? Maybe it's not us. Maybe it's you.

jokes.text: If she hits me when she is happy, can you imagine how hard she'll hit when I take away the Joey love?
jokes.setup: Joey explains the logic behind the sweater padding.
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'the Joey love' — Joey referring to himself in the third person as a romantic commodity — is both absurd and very Joey.
jokes.explanation: 'The Joey love' is a quintessential Joey line — egotistical, oddly endearing, and delivered with total sincerity. The logic (pre-padding for breakup retaliation) is both absurd and internally consistent, which is the best kind of Joey humor. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Katie, you're just too much sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Katie
dialogue.line: Too much? I'll show you too much!

jokes.text: Oh, right. I forgot that you call it that.
jokes.setup: Joey has referred to his romantic appeal as 'the Joey love.'
jokes.punchline: Rachel's response implies this is a known, recurring thing Joey says — she forgot he calls it that, confirming it's established behavior.
jokes.explanation: A perfect topper to joke 44. Rachel's casual acceptance and slight embarrassment at having forgotten Joey's term adds a layer — this is an established part of his personality. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, you have to choose. It's me or them!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Don't make me do this, Rach.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Choose!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay... how much time do I have to decide?

jokes.text: Hey, cute jacket. — Thanks. — That's so sweet! [Katie punches Rachel]
jokes.setup: Joey has warned Rachel about Katie's hitting. Rachel is about to receive a 'playful' punch.
jokes.punchline: Katie thanks Rachel for a compliment with an enthusiastic punch — confirming the problem is universal, not just Joey-specific.
jokes.explanation: The running gag spreading to Rachel is a good escalation. It confirms the problem while expanding the circle of victims, which is structurally sound for a physical comedy subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I was trying to help you! I was telling Emily how you felt!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you made me sound like a monster!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know! I don't know how that happened. I was going for sympathetic and somehow you ended up worse!

jokes.text: Joey, unable to tell Katie to stop hitting Rachel, tells Rachel he 'talked her up' — Katie hits Rachel again.
jokes.setup: Katie punches Rachel for the first time. Joey should intervene but can't bring himself to tell his girlfriend to stop.
jokes.punchline: Instead of stopping it, Joey compounds it by saying nice things about Rachel to Katie, triggering another enthusiastic punch — his fix makes things worse.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the physical comedy bit — each compliment triggers another painful punch, making Joey's social cowardice the driver of the gag. Character-consistent: Joey can't face discomfort, so he inadvertently creates more.

dialogue.speaker: Steve
dialogue.line: You cut Howard's cake?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It was an accident!

jokes.text: She just kicked me.
jokes.setup: Joey is now in the process of breaking up with Katie. He has his extra sweater padding on.
jokes.punchline: Despite all preparation, Katie still got him — this time with a kick instead of a punch, suggesting the padding was insufficient anyway.
jokes.explanation: The defeated understatement of 'She just kicked me' — especially since he padded for punches but not kicks — is a good beat. Economy is high.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, Ross is great! He's really smart and funny and sensitive!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Just last week he tried to explain his paleontology work to me and I understood almost none of it, but he kept going for like forty-five minutes anyway!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And he's super considerate - he always remembers to tell us about his weekend plans whether we ask or not!

jokes.text: Aren't you going to do something? — Do something or I'll walk out that door right now. — Are you going to?
jokes.setup: Joey is being kicked by Katie during the breakup and whispers to Rachel for help. Rachel delivers an ultimatum.
jokes.punchline: Joey calls Rachel's bluff — 'Are you going to?' — suggesting he'd actually be fine with her leaving rather than intervening.
jokes.explanation: Joey's resigned 'Are you going to?' while being abused is a quietly funny bit of cowardice. The reversal of who's threatening whom is handled economically.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so when I first met Monica, I thought she was a high-strung, controlling neat freak.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: When I first met Chandler, I thought he was a sarcastic jerk with commitment issues.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: When I first met Ross, I thought he was a boring paleontologist who only cared about dinosaurs.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: When I first met Rachel, I thought she was a spoiled, vapid princess who didn't know how to do anything.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And when I first met Joey, I thought he was a dumb, struggling actor who couldn't even read.

jokes.text: I told them about you and Emily. Trying to get some sympathy. But you came off as the bad guy. — I told it wrong.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been trying to help Ross at his party by telling his story.
jokes.punchline: Despite the fact that Ross genuinely was wronged in the Emily situation, he still came off as the bad guy — suggesting it's not the story but Ross himself that's the problem. His response ('I told it wrong') is a classic self-deceptive dodge.
jokes.explanation: 'I told it wrong' is a great Ross line — he is constitutionally incapable of accepting that he might actually be at fault, so the story must have been told incorrectly. Character-specific and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? What did I say?

jokes.text: We should talk about that because I don't understand what happened there.
jokes.setup: Ross says he told the Emily story wrong.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe, with complete sincerity, says she also doesn't understand what happened with Emily — a wink to the audience about the complexity of that storyline.
jokes.explanation: Mildly meta — Phoebe voicing audience confusion about the Emily plot. Works as a light aside. Not particularly crafted but lands with audiences who followed the season arc.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, if you insult people first, then when they insult you back, it's not an original thought!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not... that's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Isn't it though?

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Someone cut Howard's cake!
jokes.setup: Ross was eating cake at the party, trying to feel better.
jokes.punchline: The discovery that Ross ate Howard's retirement cake is treated as a major social crime — escalating his social failure to a new level.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation beat in Ross's party subplot. Each new social failure is worse than the last, and eating the man's cake — the man he refused to honor — is a satisfying ironic touch.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: This is insane.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like a car crash.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What is happening right now?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, I love you. Will you marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: This is the worst proposal I've ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But we can't stop watching.

jokes.text: 3B. You got your free food. You ruined everyone's fun. Isn't it time you went home? Go back to 3B, 3B.
jokes.setup: Ross is confronted after cutting the cake. The neighbor reduces him to his apartment number.
jokes.punchline: Being called '3B' rather than by name — reduced to a unit number at his own party — is a small but effective humiliation joke.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Go back to 3B, 3B' is a nicely specific and humiliating dismissal. Ross has become so disliked he's been reduced to a room number.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Is 'sorry' the best reason to get married?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No. The number one reason to get married is because you want to spend the rest of your life with that person.

jokes.text: Who here likes Ross? [Silence/no hands] — Of course you don't like him. He didn't give you any money. — He raised his own hand when I asked, 'Who likes Ross?' — And he's wearing two nametags.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to defend Ross to his neighbors by asking who likes him.
jokes.punchline: Three compounding revelations: (1) nobody likes him, (2) Ross raised his own hand to the question of who likes Ross, and (3) he's wearing two nametags — suggesting he put on a second one in a desperate bid to be more likeable.
jokes.explanation: A three-part escalating joke with each reveal funnier than the last. The two nametags detail is inspired — small, specific, and deeply pathetic in the best comedy way. Well-structured escalation with good character integration (only Ross would be this desperate).

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so I have a complete ranking system. A baby is number one. Then comes 'I'm dying,' then 'I'm moving to London,' then 'I'm sorry.'

jokes.text: I'll be honest. When I first met Ross, I didn't like him at all. Once I got to know him, I saw that he is really sweet and caring and very generous. All I'm saying is, don't judge Ross before you get to know him. — You know, I like all of you guys now. But when I first met you, you know? Kurt? I thought, abrasive drunk. Lola? Mind-numbingly stupid. You guys. Gold digger, cradle-robbing perv. So I think you all know what I mean.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to defend Ross by sharing that her first impression was wrong. She pivots to sharing first impressions of the other neighbors.
jokes.punchline: Each first impression is more brutal than the last — 'abrasive drunk,' 'mind-numbingly stupid,' 'gold digger, cradle-robbing perv' — each delivered with cheerful sincerity as though they're compliments in context.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode — possibly the standout. The structure is perfect: Phoebe sets up a sincere, well-intentioned defense of Ross, then pivots into insulting every single neighbor with escalating specificity. The key is that she doesn't understand why this is backfiring — she thinks she's being helpful. 'Gold digger, cradle-robbing perv' as a double-barreled insult for a couple, delivered with the same warmth as the Ross praise, is exceptional. This is elite Phoebe writing: her unique brand of unfiltered honesty colliding with a situation that requires the opposite.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, this is awkward.

jokes.text: Kurt? I thought, abrasive drunk. / Lola? Mind-numbingly stupid. / You guys. Gold digger, cradle-robbing perv.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to explain that first impressions can be wrong. She uses examples of when she first met the neighbors.
jokes.punchline: Instead of vague 'I misjudged you' examples, she delivers brutally specific first-impression insults: 'abrasive drunk,' 'mind-numbingly stupid,' 'gold digger, cradle-robbing perv' — to the actual people she's describing, to their faces.
jokes.explanation: The episode's strongest extended joke sequence. The structure is impeccable: Phoebe sets up a universal 'don't judge a book by its cover' speech, then proceeds to read every cover aloud with brutal specificity. The escalation from 'abrasive drunk' to 'mind-numbingly stupid' to the hyphenated three-parter 'gold digger, cradle-robbing perv' is perfect escalating comedy. That she means this as a compliment ('I got past these first impressions!') while saying it to their faces is the crowning irony. Very Phoebe, very wrong, perfectly constructed. Scores 8.5 on craft — comparable to the anchor examples in structure and payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So how long are you guys gonna tease me about the proposal?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, according to my calculations... the rest of your life.

jokes.text: Obviously, I didn't think they would throw things. — I thought if I kept insulting them you'd defend them. Then you'd look like the hero. — See, I did not get that.
jokes.setup: Things have been thrown at Phoebe and Ross after the insult speech.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe explains her logic — she was trying to make Ross look good by being a foil for him to defend. Ross's 'I did not get that' admits he had no idea this was a strategy.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Phoebe had a plan — however bizarre — recontextualizes joke 54 and adds a layer. Ross's admission that he didn't get it is an honest, funny beat.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We were on a break!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, will you marry me?

jokes.text: I guess there's only one way to do this. [Chandler gets on one knee]
jokes.setup: Chandler has told Monica he's been thinking about 'us' and says there's only one way to do this — building toward a sincere romantic gesture.
jokes.punchline: He gets on one knee to propose marriage — but the joke is the CONTEXT: this is Chandler, who was just having a panic attack about commitment 20 minutes ago, now doing the most extreme commitment act possible.
jokes.explanation: The proposal itself is a visual gag — the audience sees the extreme overcorrection. 'What a bad idea' and 'I can't not look at it' from onlookers confirm the audience's reaction is built into the scene. The comedic weight here is the gap between his earlier panic and this gesture.

jokes.text: What a bad idea. — I can't not look at it.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just proposed marriage on one knee.
jokes.punchline: Joey's instant assessment ('what a bad idea') and Monica's admission that she can't look away from the ring capture the audience's shared reaction — horror and fascination.
jokes.explanation: Two short reactions that efficiently voice the audience's feelings. Joey's bluntness ('what a bad idea') is perfect, and Monica's contradictory 'can't not look at it' adds a layer of dark fascination.

jokes.text: I'm doing this because I'm sorry?
jokes.setup: Monica asks why Chandler is proposing. He initially says 'I don't know' then tries to find a reason.
jokes.punchline: He lands on 'I'm sorry' as the reason for a marriage proposal, phrased as a question — suggesting even he doesn't believe this logic.
jokes.explanation: The phrasing as a question is the key — Chandler is so confused by his own behavior that he can't even commit to the reason. Very character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: Do you think the best reason to get married is because you're sorry? The best reason is pregnancy. Sorry is fourth, behind being ready and actually wanting to get married.
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Chandler's 'sorry' reasoning for proposing.
jokes.punchline: Monica has a ranked list of reasons to get married, with pregnancy at #1 and 'sorry' at #4 — delivered as though this is an obvious taxonomy she's always had ready.
jokes.explanation: Monica's ranked list of marriage reasons is a great joke — specifically that pregnancy beats 'being ready' at #1, and 'sorry' comes after three better options. The specificity of naming the rankings makes this feel fresh rather than generic. Very Monica in its organized, opinionated delivery.

jokes.text: Who? Two divorces and Joey?
jokes.setup: Chandler explains that he talked to 'these guys' and got confused. Monica asks who he talked to.
jokes.punchline: Monica's summary of Chandler's advisors — 'two divorces and Joey' — is a devastating quick assessment of why taking their advice on relationships was a bad idea.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Two divorces and Joey' reduces Ross and Rachel's complicated relationship histories to a devastating credential check in five words. The comedy comes from the accuracy — she's completely right that these are not ideal relationship advisors. Perfect economy, high quotability, works as a standalone line.

jokes.text: Who? Two divorces and Joey?
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals he got his advice about Monica from Ross and Joey. Monica asks who.
jokes.punchline: Monica's summary dismissal: 'Two divorces and Joey' — identifying both the specific disqualifying flaw (Ross's marital history) and the general disqualifying flaw (being Joey) in four words.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Perfect economy — four words that contain a devastating logical argument against their qualifications as relationship advisors. 'Two divorces' is specific (Ross's track record) and 'Joey' needs no explanation — his name alone is the disqualifier. The asymmetry (a data point vs. just a name) is very funny. This line is quotable, economical, and character-perfect for Monica's withering intelligence. Comparable to the '8.0 anchor' in economy and punch.

jokes.text: She's right, you know? — Yeah, but still, cheap shot!
jokes.setup: Monica has just said 'two divorces and Joey.'
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately concedes ('she's right') and Joey, also conceding she's right, still calls it a cheap shot — unable to deny the accuracy.
jokes.explanation: The perfect topper to joke 60. Ross conceding immediately is funny; Joey calling it a cheap shot while also conceding it's accurate is funnier. The two reactions together make this a strong beat.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. What would you have done if I had said yes? — I would've been happy because I would spend the rest of my life with the woman I love. — Or you would have seen a Chandler-shaped hole in that door.
jokes.setup: Monica challenges Chandler to consider what would have happened if she'd accepted his panic proposal.
jokes.punchline: Chandler gives a sincere, romantic answer — then Monica proposes the alternative: a 'Chandler-shaped hole in that door,' implying he would have fled through the wall.
jokes.explanation: 'A Chandler-shaped hole in that door' is a vivid, cartoon-physics image that perfectly encapsulates Chandler's commitment phobia. The setup (his sincere romantic answer) makes the punchline land harder by contrast. High quotability and character integration — this only works for Chandler.

jokes.text: Will you pass that knife? — No, I will not. — You don't have to be mean about it. — You're right. I'm sorry. Will you marry me?
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey are at the table. Ross asks for a knife. Joey refuses and is told he's being mean.
jokes.punchline: Joey apologizes — then immediately follows the apology with 'Will you marry me?' — echoing the Chandler proposal pattern and ribbing both Ross and Chandler simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Joey repurposing the 'sorry = propose' logic for a mundane knife-passing situation is a great callback. The escalation of a small social moment into a marriage proposal mirrors Chandler's panic perfectly.

jokes.text: I was going to ask you to marry me because I didn't say hello to you.
jokes.setup: The table is now ribbing Chandler by applying the proposal logic everywhere. Ross has another application.
jokes.punchline: Ross's escalation — that the apology-proposal logic would apply even to not saying hello — further satirizes how absurd Chandler's reasoning was.
jokes.explanation: Extends the running gag but with diminishing returns. Still funny but less sharp than the Joey version above.

jokes.text: Or ask them to move in with you. But I'm not sure. Chandler?
jokes.setup: The group is riffing on what constitutes a proposal-worthy offense.
jokes.punchline: Ross throws in 'move in with you' as another possible sorry-gesture, then turns to Chandler for verification — asking the man who just failed a proposal to confirm the apology-to-commitment scale.
jokes.explanation: The 'Chandler?' turn — asking him as the acknowledged expert on this absurd relationship dynamic — is a good button. Slightly overstays the gag but Chandler's response saves it.

jokes.text: How long is this going to go on? — I think the length of teasing is directly related to how insane you were. So a long time.
jokes.setup: Chandler wants the teasing about his proposal to end.
jokes.punchline: Monica's formula — teasing duration proportional to insanity level — with the conclusion 'so a long time' is a confident, satisfying closer.
jokes.explanation: Monica's crisp logic — teasing is proportional to insanity — and the coda 'so a long time' is a clean, satisfying button on the episode's main comic thread.

jokes.text: Remember that 'we were on a break' thing? — I'm sorry. Will you marry me?
jokes.setup: Joey applies the sorry-proposal to Ross's most infamous ongoing grievance — the 'we were on a break' argument.
jokes.punchline: Joey proposes to Ross over the break argument — the callback to a multi-season running joke lands as a perfect final button on the episode.
jokes.explanation: A double callback — to Chandler's sorry-proposal and to the series' most iconic running gag. The synthesis is clever and satisfying. 'I'm sorry. Will you marry me?' applied to the 'we were on a break' argument is a perfect series-aware button. High quotability for fans of the show.

jokes.text: That's not funny.
jokes.setup: Joey has just proposed to Ross over 'we were on a break.'
jokes.punchline: Ross's humorless 'That's not funny' — delivered while everyone around him finds it very funny — is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: A reliable final button — Ross's indignation is the punchline. Classic sitcom close. Economy perfect, originality low.

tmdb_overview: Joey starts dating Katie, a little girl who packs a mean punch.  When Ross refuses to contribute to the retirement fund of the building's maintenance man, he winds up offending everyone in the building. Meanwhile, Chandler freaks out about his relationship with Monica.
insight: Joey's dating disasters drive 22 of 61 jokes—character comedy at its densest.
